title: Russian arrested on charges he spied on and harassed employees of defense tech company Palantir | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

A Russian man was arrested in the US and charged in October with stalking and harassing employees of the defense tech giant Palantir because of its assistance to Ukraine in the war with Russia, two sources familiar with the case say.

The man, Igor D’iu, believed he was gathering information for “the Motherland,” according to court documents. He faces charges including acting as an agent of a foreign government, interstate stalking and fraud.

While court documents do not identify the company targeted in D’iu’s alleged operation, two sources familiar with the case identified it as Palantir, a tech firm with deep US government ties which has provided Ukraine with software to identify Russian targets, guide military operations and investigate war crimes.

According to the Justice Department, D’iu was working with unnamed co-conspirators when he snuck into the US through Mexico over the summer. The co-conspirators, which he spoke to only through an encrypted messaging app, provided him with instructions, equipment, and money, the department said.

Their work, the co-conspirators allegedly told D’iu, was to collect evidence on Palantir because of its help to Ukraine. Two sources familiar with the matter said the goal was to “get into the company’s systems” as opposed to targeting individuals, and that they were ultimately unsuccessful.

The indictment comes as the country grapples with other foreign efforts to obtain American technology. And while similar attempts have long been conducted abroad, D’iu’s indictment marks the first time that a foreign national has tried to access Palantir’s networks from US soil, one of the people said.

To that end, D’iu allegedly conducted surveillance on some Palantir employees, looking up their addresses and following them as they left the office. One person familiar with the matter told CNN that D’iu researched employees at all levels of the organization and did not appear to target anyone specifically.

In one instance highlighted by prosecutors, D’iu followed a woman in her car for almost 30 miles. She attempted to lose his tail by “making irregular turns, taking back roads, and entering a grocery store parking lot,” the department said, but he took illegal turns and ran red lights to keep her in his sights.

D’iu was later confronted by police over the incident, prosecutors said, and told them he followed the woman because he thought she was beautiful and wanted to ask her out on a date.

Palantir employees also reported it to law enforcement, and the company began cooperating with the FBI, one of the sources said.

In a separate incident, D’iu was allegedly told to visit a coffee shop near Palantir’s offices in Palo Alto, California, photograph employees’ laptop screens, and send the images to his co-conspirators. Two days later, he was told to return with his own laptop so they could remotely control it and try to collect data from nearby employees’ devices, prosecutors said.

“Trolling 28-year-old employees at their coffee shop to try to look at their networks is what modern warfare is, and companies that are in the middle of this will be targeted,” one of the sources said. “That’s just the new way it’s working. And you know, it’s sadly come home to America.”

The work gradually increased, court documents say, and D’iu would bring his laptop to different locations in the area for hours at a time.

When agents searched his apartment in Palo Alto and his devices, they found lists of employee addresses, their relatives’ names, as well as “assessments of leadership qualities, strengths and weaknesses,” according to court documents. Agents also found two Russian passports, fraudulent identification documents and $18,000 in cash.

A lawyer for D’iu was not listed on the court docket.
